Getting started with ASMap

Source: vignettes/articles/getting-started.Rmd
getting-started.Rmd

ASMap constructs genetic linkage maps using the MSTmap algorithm, which clusters markers into linkage groups and orders the markers within each group in a single pass. This article builds a map from scratch and points at the rest of the documentation.

Installation 

install.packages("ASMap")

# development version
# install.packages("devtools")
devtools::install_github("DrJ001/ASMap")

Building a map from marker scores

The package datasets are not lazy-loaded, so they need an explicit data() call. mapDHf is an unconstructed doubled haploid wheat marker set, in the layout the construction function expects: markers in rows, genotypes in columns, with marker names in the rownames and genotype names in the names.

library(ASMap)
data(mapDHf)

dim(mapDHf)
[1] 599 218
mapDHf[1:5, 1:6]
        DH1 DH2 DH3 DH4 DH5 DH6
5B.m.2    B   B   B   A   A   B
5A.m.52   B   B   A   A   B   A
2B.m.1    A   B   A   B   B   A
6B.m.3    B   B   A   B   A   A
5A.m.43   B   B   A   B   B   A

One call clusters the markers into linkage groups, orders them within each group and estimates the genetic distances.

map <- mstmap(mapDHf, pop.type = "DH", dist.fun = "kosambi", p.value = 1e-06)
Number of linkage groups: 24
The size of the linkage groups are: 56  54  35  41  4   37  6   30  40  27  37  13  15  10  21  6   32  33  33  41  6   9   5   8   
The number of bins in each linkage group: 55    53  34  41  3   36  6   29  40  27  36  13  14  9   21  5   32  33  32  41  5   8   4   7   
nchr(map)
[1] 24
round(chrlen(map), 1)
   L1    L2    L3    L4    L5    L6    L7    L8    L9   L10   L11   L12   L13 
142.8 181.9  97.4 115.4  21.7 108.2  13.3 133.9 153.2  98.7 145.8  60.4  72.2 
  L14   L15   L16   L17   L18   L19   L20   L21   L22   L23   L24 
 81.2  98.2   8.7 109.5  60.9 134.5 104.0  18.0   7.8   7.8  19.2

Starting from an existing cross object

If the markers are already in a cross object, the same generic accepts it. bychr = FALSE bulks every marker and rebuilds the map from scratch, ignoring the existing linkage groups.

data(mapDH)
map2 <- mstmap(mapDH, bychr = FALSE, dist.fun = "kosambi", p.value = 1e-06)
Number of linkage groups: 24
The size of the linkage groups are: 41  5   33  10  40  35  8   13  37  30  6   9   21  32  6   54  56  6   27  41  15  33  37  4   
The number of bins in each linkage group: 41    4   33  9   40  34  7   13  36  29  5   8   21  32  6   53  55  5   27  41  14  32  36  3   
nchr(map2)
[1] 24

Setting bychr = TRUE instead keeps the existing groups and only re-orders the markers within them. Two settings are worth committing to memory:

# cluster and order from scratch, ignoring existing linkage groups
mstmap(cross, bychr = FALSE, p.value = 1e-12)

# re-order within existing linkage groups, never splitting them
mstmap(cross, bychr = TRUE, p.value = 2)

A p.value greater than 1 switches clustering off altogether, which is what makes the second idiom work.

Choosing p.value

p.value sets the threshold at which markers are split into separate linkage groups, and the right value depends strongly on population size — larger populations need a smaller one. Expect to try a few. pValue() plots the relationship, so the choice can be made deliberately rather than by trial and error.

pValue(dist = c(25, 30, 35, 40), pop.size = 100:500, map.function = "kosambi")

For a population of around 300, a p.value of 1e-12 gives a threshold of roughly 30 cM before markers are linked into the same group.

Checking the result

heatMap() shows pairwise recombination fractions and LOD scores of linkage together, each with its own legend. Consistent heat within a linkage group means the markers near each other really are linked.

heatMap(mapDH, lmax = 50)
